description: How World War II rebuilt US industry, and the suburban boom and 'poverty amidst plenty' of the 1950s.
content_html:
America Goes to War: The Wartime Economy

When Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, the USA entered the Second World War. The effect on the American economy was transformational. Factories that had made cars switched to producing tanks and aircraft. By 1944, the USA was manufacturing more war material than all the Axis powers combined. Unemployment — still around 14 per cent in 1940 — effectively disappeared as millions entered the armed forces and the defence industries absorbed the rest.

Key Fact

The Second World War ended the Great Depression more decisively than the New Deal had. By 1944, unemployment had fallen to below 2 per cent as 12 million Americans served in the armed forces and defence production boomed. GDP roughly doubled between 1939 and 1945.

Women and Minorities in the Wartime Workforce

With men away at war, women entered the workforce in unprecedented numbers. The image of Rosie the Riveter became a symbol of women’s wartime contribution. By 1944 around 19 million women held jobs, including in heavy industry. African American workers also moved north and west in large numbers — the so-called Great Migration accelerated — taking factory jobs in Detroit, Chicago and Los Angeles. Executive Order 8802 (1941), issued by President Roosevelt, banned racial discrimination in defence industries, though enforcement was uneven.

The GI Bill (1944), formally the Servicemen’s Readjustment Act, reshaped post-war America. It gave returning veterans access to low-cost mortgages, funding for college education, and small business loans. Around 8 million veterans used the education benefits, swelling university enrolments and creating a better-educated workforce. Cheap mortgages enabled millions of families to buy homes — fuelling the suburban expansion of the late 1940s and 1950s.

However, the GI Bill’s benefits were distributed unequally. African American veterans faced discrimination from banks that refused mortgages and from universities that denied admission. The bill inadvertently reinforced racial segregation in housing by making all-white suburbs accessible to white veterans while largely excluding Black Americans.

The Suburban Dream: Levittown and the 1950s Boom

Post-war prosperity transformed where and how Americans lived. Developer William Levitt mass-produced entire communities of affordable homes. Levittown (New York, from 1947) offered identical houses at prices veterans could afford with GI Bill mortgages. The car made commuting practical, and by the mid-1950s millions of families had left cities for the suburbs. Between 1950 and 1960, suburban populations grew by over 40 per cent.

Key Fact

The 1950s saw the rise of a consumer society: television ownership rose from around 9 per cent of homes in 1950 to nearly 90 per cent by 1960. Car ownership, refrigerators, washing machines and drive-in cinemas defined the decade. GDP grew strongly and real wages rose, giving many Americans a standard of living unprecedented in history.

Consumer Society and its Contradictions

The 1950s economy was powered by mass consumption. Advertisers used television to create demand for new products. Credit became widely available, and the concept of “keeping up with the Joneses” — matching neighbours’ material possessions — became a cultural force. The economy grew rapidly, and by the late 1950s the USA produced roughly half the world’s manufactured goods.

The interstate highway system, authorised by President Eisenhower in the Federal Aid Highway Act of 1956, was the largest public works project in American history. Over 41,000 miles of motorway were planned, linking every major city and transforming the movement of goods, people and military equipment. The highways deepened car dependency, gave a further boost to the automobile industry, and accelerated the shift of retail and employment from city centres to suburban sites. Shopping centres and drive-through restaurants became defining features of American culture during this decade.

Beneath the prosperity, deep inequalities persisted. In 1962, journalist and activist Michael Harrington published The Other America, arguing that between 40 and 50 million Americans — roughly a quarter of the population — lived in poverty invisible to the suburban mainstream. These were the rural poor of Appalachia, elderly Americans on fixed incomes, African Americans excluded from the post-war boom, and urban workers left behind by economic change.

The phrase “poverty amidst plenty” captured the paradox: the world’s wealthiest nation contained millions who could not afford adequate food, housing or healthcare. Harrington’s book influenced President Kennedy and contributed directly to President Johnson’s “War on Poverty” in the mid-1960s, which created Medicare, Medicaid and federal education funding through the Great Society programme.
exam_tip_html: For 8-mark “Explain Change” questions on the US economy, always show the direction of change — e.g. from mass unemployment in 1933 to full employment by 1944 — and explain what caused the shift. For 16-mark period essays comparing the 1930s and 1950s economies, link causes to consequences clearly: war spending caused economic recovery; GI Bill mortgages caused suburbanisation; but persistent racial inequality meant the post-war boom was unevenly shared.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Second World War transformed the US economy, ending the Great Depression as defence production and military service absorbed the unemployed. By 1944 unemployment had fallen to below 2 per cent.
  • The GI Bill (1944) and cheap mortgages fuelled 1950s suburbanisation and consumerism — TV ownership, cars and appliances symbolised the post-war boom — but benefits were distributed unequally along racial lines.
  • Michael Harrington’s The Other America (1962) exposed that up to 50 million Americans lived in poverty despite national prosperity — the concept of “poverty amidst plenty” that would shape 1960s social policy.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the wartime economy in the USA after 1941.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names a feature (e.g. rapid conversion of factories to war production) AND develops it (e.g. car plants began making tanks and aircraft; by 1944 the USA produced more war material than all Axis powers combined). Developing: Identifies feature without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of American suburban life in the 1950s.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) Mass-produced housing communities like Levittown made home ownership affordable for veterans using GI Bill mortgages; (2) Consumer goods such as televisions and cars became widespread, with TV ownership rising from 9% to nearly 90% of homes in the decade. Developing: Identifies features without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of American suburbs in the 1950s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (GI Bill mortgages; Levittown-style mass building; car ownership enabling commuting; wartime savings) AND explains through a developed chain of reasoning how this cause led to suburban expansion. Secure: Cause with some development. Developing: Simple statement. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Michael Harrington publishing The Other America in 1962.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (influenced Kennedy and then Johnson's War on Poverty; drew public attention to hidden poverty; challenged the myth that 1950s prosperity was universal) AND explains the chain of effects with development. Secure: Consequence identified with some development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the GI Bill (1944) for the development of post-war America.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (enabled veterans to buy homes, attend college, start businesses; fuelled suburban growth; created better-educated workforce) AND over time (reinforced racial inequalities as Black veterans were largely excluded; shaped American middle-class identity; contributed to 1950s prosperity). Secure: One time frame covered. Developing: Describes the GI Bill without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: 'The post-war economic boom of the 1950s benefited all Americans equally.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge of the period 1944-1965.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing evidence for and against with a substantiated judgement. FOR: GDP growth; TV/car ownership rising; suburban expansion; GI Bill opportunities. AGAINST: GI Bill discriminatory in practice; Levittown initially refused Black residents; Harrington's 40-50 million in poverty; Appalachian poor; elderly on fixed incomes; African Americans excluded from union jobs. Overall judgement must be argued, not listed. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Limited evidence, one-sided. Emerging: Narrative only.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the name of the mass-produced suburban community built in New York state from 1947?
What did Michael Harrington's 1962 book The Other America argue?
options: Millions of Americans still lived in poverty despite national prosperity
The GI Bill had created an equal society

knowledge_checks.q: The cultural icon _____ represented women who entered defence industry jobs while men served overseas.
The _____ Bill of 1944 provided returning veterans with low-cost mortgages and college tuition funding.
Match each term to its description:
right: Gave veterans mortgages, education grants and business loans
Author who exposed poverty among 40-50 million Americans in 1962
Symbol of women working in wartime defence industries

flashcard_questions.q: When did the USA enter the Second World War?
flashcard_questions.a: 7 December 1941, following the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to US unemployment by 1944?
flashcard_questions.a: It fell to below 2 per cent as defence production and military service absorbed workers.
A cultural icon representing women who took up industrial jobs during the Second World War.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the GI Bill (1944) provide for veterans?
flashcard_questions.a: Low-cost mortgages, college tuition funding, and small business loans.
A mass-produced suburban community built in New York state from 1947.

flashcard_questions.q: By what percentage did suburban populations grow between 1950 and 1960?
What share of homes had a television in the USA by 1960?
How many Americans did Harrington estimate lived in poverty in the early 1960s?
flashcard_questions.a: Between 40 and 50 million — roughly a quarter of the population.

flashcard_questions.q: What phrase describes the paradox of widespread poverty in a wealthy 1950s USA?

flashcard_questions.a: Roosevelt's order banning racial discrimination in defence industries.

glossary_terms.definition: A cultural icon of the Second World War representing women who worked in defence industries while men served overseas.
The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, which provided veterans with low-cost mortgages, college tuition, business loans and unemployment pay.
A planned suburban community built in New York state from 1947, becoming a symbol of post-war American suburbanisation.
An American writer whose 1962 book The Other America exposed persistent poverty among tens of millions of Americans, helping to inspire the War on Poverty.
